steps.body: One chapter left to close Grade 7 geometry: putting it all together. Scale drawings convert, circles measure, angle facts become equations, side lengths decide triangles, and cuts reveal cross-sections.
steps.narration: One chapter left to close Grade 7 geometry: putting it all together. Scale drawings convert, circles measure, angle facts become equations, side lengths decide triangles, and cuts reveal cross-sections.

widget.prompt: On a 1 cm = 2 m plan, a circular fountain has a drawing radius of 3 cm. What is its real radius, in meters?

choices.label: 6 m
choices.feedback: The scale chain is exact: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

choices.label: 3 m
choices.feedback: That's the drawing radius — convert with the scale: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

choices.label: 12 m
choices.feedback: That doubled twice (or used the diameter) — the radius converts once: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Drawing → real multiplies by the scale: 3 × 2 = 6 m.
widget.successFeedback: The scale chain is exact: 3 × 2 = 6 m.

predict.prompt: Drawing radius 3 cm on a 1 cm = 2 m plan (real radius 6 m). Is the real area just 2 × the drawing's area number?

options.label: Areas don't scale with the plan

predict.reveal: Lengths scale ×2 but areas ×4: the drawing's 9 × π becomes a real 36 × π. Converting the radius first (3 cm → 6 m, then π × r^2) dodges the trap automatically — scale the length, then square.

steps.body: Skills chain together. That 6 m radius feeds straight into the circle formulas: circumference C = 2 × π × 6 = 12 × π meters of fence, area A = π × 6^2 = 36 × π square meters of water.
steps.narration: Skills chain together. That 6 m radius feeds straight into the circle formulas: circumference C = 2 × π × 6 = 12 × π meters of fence, area A = π × 6^2 = 36 × π square meters of water.

widget.prompt: The real fountain has radius 6 m. What is k in C = k × π meters of fencing?

choices.label: 12 × π m
choices.feedback: C = 2 × π × r, so 2 × 6 = 12 × π meters.

choices.label: 36 × π m
choices.feedback: That's r^2 (the area) — fencing follows the circumference: 2 × 6 = 12 × π.

choices.label: 6 × π m
choices.feedback: That's the radius — C = 2 × π × r doubles it: 12 × π.

widget.successFeedback: C = 2 × π × r, so 2 × 6 = 12 × π meters.

steps.body: Slice the pyramid in the design.

widget.prompt: The garden design also includes a small square pyramid. A cut is made straight down through its tip. What is the cross-section?

options.label: A triangle
options.feedback: Right — a cut straight down through the apex slices two triangular faces, giving a triangular cross-section.

options.label: A smaller square
options.feedback: A smaller square comes from a cut parallel to the base — a cut through the tip gives a triangle.

options.label: A circle
options.feedback: A pyramid has flat sides, not curved ones — the tip cut gives a triangle, not a circle.

options.label: The same-size square
options.feedback: The tip cut runs vertically through the apex, not parallel to the base — that gives a triangle, not a square.

explanationVariants: The two path angles fill a straight line: x + 2x = 180 → 3x = 180 → x = 60.

widget.prompt: Two garden paths meet the fountain's edge, making angles x and 2x on a straight line. Solve for x (in degrees).

commonAngles.feedback: That solved 2x = 180 — combine both terms: 3x = 180, so x = 60.
A straight line holds 180°, not 90°: 3x = 180, x = 60.

widget.successFeedback: The two parts now fill the straight line: 60° + 120° = 180°.

explanationVariants: 7 + 8 = 15 beats 12, so the three beams close into a triangle.

widget.prompt: A triangular trellis needs beams of 7, 8, and 12 feet. Will they form a triangle?

choices.label: Yes — 7 + 8 = 15 beats 12
choices.feedback: Right — the shorter pair out-reaches the longest beam, so the frame closes.

choices.label: No — 12 is too long
choices.feedback: Check the sum: 7 + 8 = 15 > 12, so the beams do close into a triangle.

choices.label: No — the sides differ
choices.feedback: Different sides are fine — 7 + 8 > 12 passes the triangle test.

choices.label: Only if 12 is the base
choices.feedback: Position doesn't matter — 7 + 8 > 12 works regardless of which beam is the base.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Compare 7 + 8 with 12. The shorter pair must strictly out-reach the longest beam.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the shorter pair out-reaches the longest beam, so the frame closes.

explanationVariants: Real radius: 2 × 2 = 4 m. Area: π × 4^2 = 16 × π m^2.

widget.prompt: A second fountain has drawing radius 2 cm at 1 cm = 2 m. What is k in its real area A = k × π square meters?

choices.label: 16 × π m^2
choices.feedback: The real radius is 4 m, and 4^2 = 16, so the area is 16 × π m^2.

choices.label: 4 × π m^2
choices.feedback: That's the real radius (2 × 2 = 4 m) — now square it for area: 16 × π.

choices.label: 8 × π m^2
choices.feedback: That's the circumference (2 × 4) — area squares the radius: 4^2 = 16 × π.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Real radius: 2 × 2 = 4 m. A = π × r^2 = 16 × π m^2.
widget.successFeedback: The real radius is 4 m, and 4^2 = 16, so the area is 16 × π m^2.

hints: Convert the radius to real meters first: 2 cm × 2 m per cm.
Real radius = 4 m. Area squares it.

steps.body: Scale, circles, angles, triangles, and slices — Grade 7 geometry, complete.
takeaways: Convert with the scale first, then apply circle formulas.
Angle facts become equations; side sums decide triangles.
You now hold every 7.G tool — and the π × r^2 behind Grade 8's volumes.
steps.teaser: That completes Grade 7 Geometry — and with it, all five Grade 7 domains.

concept.body: Chain the skills: convert lengths with the scale first (drawing → real multiplies), then use the circle formulas — C = 2 × π × r doubles the radius, A = π × r^2 squares it.
